text:
The world is in the midst of one of the most significant energy transformations in modern history. Governments, businesses, and consumers are increasingly embracing cleaner technologies in an effort to reduce carbon emissions, improve energy efficiency, and build a more sustainable future. At the center of this transition lies a technology that has quietly become indispensable to modern life: the lithium-ion battery.

From powering electric vehicles and smartphones to storing renewable energy generated by solar and wind farms, lithium-ion batteries have become the foundation of today's electrified economy. Their ability to store large amounts of energy in compact, lightweight designs has made them the preferred choice for a growing range of applications across industries.

According to Renub Research, the global Lithium-Ion Battery Market is expected to grow from US$111.33 billion in 2025 to US$562.91 billion by 2034, expanding at a remarkable compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 19.73 percent during the forecast period. This extraordinary growth reflects rising global demand for electric mobility, renewable energy storage, consumer electronics, and advanced energy solutions.

As the world accelerates toward electrification, lithium-ion batteries are becoming one of the most strategically important technologies of the twenty-first century.

Download Free Sample Report

The Technology Behind Modern Energy Storage

Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable energy storage devices that operate by moving lithium ions between positive and negative electrodes during charging and discharging cycles. Their unique chemistry allows them to deliver high energy density, long operational life, and relatively low self-discharge rates compared to traditional battery technologies.

These advantages have helped lithium-ion batteries dominate the global energy storage market. Their lightweight design and ability to provide consistent performance make them suitable for everything from smartphones and laptops to electric vehicles and industrial energy storage systems.

Unlike older battery technologies, lithium-ion batteries offer greater efficiency and improved charging capabilities. Continuous innovation has further enhanced their safety, durability, and overall performance, making them increasingly attractive for large-scale applications.

Today, lithium-ion technology is not merely supporting technological progress—it is actively enabling it.

Electric Vehicles Are Driving Unprecedented Demand

Perhaps the most important factor fueling market growth is the rapid adoption of electric vehicles.

Governments around the world are implementing policies designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and encourage cleaner transportation alternatives. Automakers are responding by investing billions of dollars in electric vehicle development, manufacturing facilities, and battery technologies.

Lithium-ion batteries remain the preferred energy source for electric vehicles because of their high energy density, long driving range, and improving cost efficiency. Modern battery systems allow vehicles to travel greater distances while supporting faster charging capabilities.

Consumer interest in electric mobility continues to grow as charging infrastructure expands and vehicle affordability improves. Beyond passenger cars, electric buses, trucks, delivery vehicles, and two-wheelers are contributing to increasing battery demand.

As transportation becomes increasingly electrified, lithium-ion batteries will remain at the heart of this transformation.

Renewable Energy Storage Is Creating New Opportunities

Another major growth driver is the expansion of renewable energy generation.

Solar and wind power are becoming increasingly important components of global energy systems. However, these energy sources are inherently variable because their output depends on weather conditions and environmental factors.

Lithium-ion batteries provide a solution by storing excess energy when production exceeds demand and releasing it when needed. This capability helps stabilize electricity grids and improves the reliability of renewable energy systems.

Large-scale battery storage projects are being deployed worldwide to support renewable energy integration and enhance grid resilience. Governments and utility companies increasingly recognize the importance of energy storage technologies in achieving long-term sustainability goals.

As investments in renewable energy continue rising, demand for lithium-ion batteries within stationary storage applications is expected to grow significantly.

Technology Improvements Are Accelerating Adoption

Continuous technological innovation has played a critical role in expanding the lithium-ion battery market.

Researchers and manufacturers are constantly working to improve battery chemistry, increase energy density, enhance safety, and reduce production costs. These improvements are making lithium-ion batteries more competitive across a wider range of applications.

Advancements in high-nickel cathodes, solid-state battery development, thermal management systems, and battery management software are helping improve overall performance. Faster charging capabilities are also addressing one of the most common concerns among electric vehicle users.

At the same time, manufacturing scale and efficiency improvements have contributed to substantial cost reductions over the past decade. Lower costs are making battery-powered technologies more accessible to consumers and businesses alike.

As innovation continues, lithium-ion batteries are expected to become even more efficient, reliable, and affordable.

Consumer Electronics Continue to Depend on Lithium-Ion Batteries

While electric vehicles often receive the most attention, consumer electronics remain a major contributor to battery demand.

Smartphones, laptops, tablets, wearable devices, wireless headphones, and numerous other electronic products rely heavily on lithium-ion technology. Consumers expect these devices to deliver long battery life, rapid charging, and reliable performance.

Lithium-ion batteries provide the energy density necessary to support increasingly sophisticated electronic devices without significantly increasing size or weight.

As global demand for connected devices continues growing, consumer electronics will remain an important market segment for battery manufacturers.

The rise of smart homes, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and portable technology is expected to create additional opportunities for battery innovation and adoption.

Different Battery Chemistries Serve Different Needs

The lithium-ion battery market includes several different chemistries, each designed to address specific performance requirements.

Lithium Cobalt Oxide batteries are widely used in consumer electronics because they offer high energy density and reliable performance. Smartphones, laptops, and tablets frequently utilize this chemistry.

Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries have gained popularity in electric vehicle and energy storage applications due to their safety, durability, and long cycle life.

Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt and Lithium Nickel Cobalt Aluminum batteries provide higher energy density and are commonly used in premium electric vehicle applications.

The diversity of battery chemistries allows manufacturers to optimize performance based on specific application requirements, helping drive broader market adoption.

Challenges Remain Despite Strong Growth

Although the outlook for the lithium-ion battery market is highly positive, several challenges remain.

One of the most significant concerns involves raw material supply. Lithium, cobalt, and nickel are critical components used in battery production, and securing reliable supplies has become increasingly important as demand grows.

Price volatility and geopolitical factors can affect the availability of these materials, creating uncertainty within supply chains. Environmental concerns related to mining operations also continue attracting attention from regulators, investors, and consumers.

Manufacturers are actively exploring alternative materials, recycling solutions, and more sustainable sourcing practices to address these challenges.

Long-term success will depend on building resilient and responsible supply chains capable of supporting continued market expansion.

Safety and Recycling Are Key Priorities

Safety remains another important consideration.

While lithium-ion batteries are generally reliable, incidents involving overheating, thermal runaway, and fire risks have highlighted the importance of robust design and manufacturing standards.

Battery manufacturers continue investing heavily in safety technologies, including advanced monitoring systems, thermal management solutions, and improved cell designs.

Recycling presents an additional challenge. As battery usage increases globally, the industry must develop efficient systems for recovering valuable materials from end-of-life products.

Battery recycling not only reduces environmental impacts but also helps strengthen supply chain sustainability by recovering critical raw materials.

Many governments and private companies are investing in recycling infrastructure to support the industry's long-term growth.

Regional Markets Are Driving Innovation

Several countries are emerging as key players within the global lithium-ion battery ecosystem.

The United States is experiencing strong growth driven by electric vehicle adoption, domestic battery manufacturing investments, and large-scale energy storage projects. Government incentives and clean energy policies continue encouraging market expansion.

The United Kingdom is focusing on decarbonization, renewable energy integration, and battery recycling technologies. Investments in sustainable supply chains are helping strengthen the market's long-term prospects.

India is rapidly expanding its battery manufacturing capabilities as electric mobility adoption increases. Government initiatives supporting domestic production are helping reduce dependence on imported technologies.

Saudi Arabia is leveraging battery storage solutions to support renewable energy projects and broader sustainability initiatives aligned with its Vision 2030 strategy.

These regional developments demonstrate the growing global importance of lithium-ion battery technology.

The Future of Energy Storage

Looking ahead, lithium-ion batteries are expected to remain the dominant energy storage technology for the foreseeable future.

Continued advances in battery chemistry, manufacturing efficiency, recycling systems, and charging infrastructure will further strengthen their position within the global energy landscape.

Emerging technologies such as solid-state batteries may unlock even greater performance improvements, while artificial intelligence and advanced software systems enhance battery management and optimization.

As electrification expands across transportation, industry, and energy sectors, demand for reliable and efficient energy storage solutions will continue growing.

Lithium-ion batteries are not simply supporting this transition—they are enabling it.

Final Thoughts

The global lithium-ion battery market is entering a period of extraordinary growth driven by electric vehicles, renewable energy expansion, technological innovation, and increasing demand for portable electronics.

With the market projected to grow from US$111.33 billion in 2025 to US$562.91 billion by 2034, lithium-ion batteries are becoming one of the most important technologies powering the modern economy. Their role extends far beyond consumer devices, influencing transportation systems, energy infrastructure, industrial operations, and sustainability initiatives worldwide.

While challenges related to raw materials, safety, and recycling remain important considerations, ongoing innovation continues creating new opportunities for growth and improvement.

As the world moves toward a cleaner, more electrified future, lithium-ion batteries will remain at the center of that transformation, powering the technologies and solutions that define the next generation of global progress.

text:
The reduction of greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) is crucial to mitigate climate change1. Renewable energies, including solar photovoltaic (PV), are key technologies to achieve the decarbonization goals1. In 2024, PV generated 7% of the global electrical energy2. Furthermore, PV capacity is growing, it is projected to triple by 20303. China accounts for nearly 60% of global renewable capacity growth, with solar PV representing 80% of its expansion4. However, from a life-cycle perspective, PV is not an emission-free technology because during the material extraction, manufacturing, transport, installation, and end of life of these systems, GHG are emitted5. Nevertheless, in 2019, the global PV market mitigated more than 4 times the GHG produced6. A previous study projected that if the deployment is focused on carbon-intensive regions and the manufacturing is prioritized in Europe and North America, the GHG mitigation could almost double by 2060 compared with other projections6. This and other scientific studies have explored the difference that the deployment strategies make in mitigating GHG globally and advocate for strategic international coordination7.

Currently, some organisations involve several countries around the world to collaborate on renewable energy deployment, such as the Race to Zero campaign8, the International Energy Agency (IEA)9, and the International Renewable energy agency (IRENA)10. On a continental level, the EU represents a successful collaboration framework with proven results, integrated policies, and substantial financial commitments. In the EU, renewable energy has reached almost a 48% share of the total electrical energy generation during 20242. REPower EU mobilized close to $300 billion for renewables and reached almost 338 GW of new solar energy capacity installed11. Therefore, the EU renewable energy framework could benefit from a deployment strategy that achieves faster decarbonization, as shown by the world-level studies6. However, a review on PV power deployment in central European countries shows that even with a variety of policy measures, a stronger influence is given by a set of national rules and financial support12.

The GHG mitigation potential from PV deployment has been assessed in previous research as the product of the PV energy generation potential and the grid carbon intensity7. The PV generation is influenced by several environmental factors that change depending on the location. Irradiance has been determined as the main factor influencing PV generation13. However, other factors such as temperature, dust and snow also affect the performance of PV systems13. Furthermore, the degradation of the PV modules, which causes a reduction of the PV generation with time, also varies depending on the environmental factors of a given location14. Regarding the lifecycle grid carbon intensity, it is calculated as the total lifecycle GHG emissions divided by the total electrical energy generated in each area of the electrical grid15.

The GHG mitigation potential of PV allocation strategies has been studied previously, on a global and national scale. One study evaluated 1 kWp of three PV technologies to determine the best manufacturer-installation scenario for providing the highest reduction in GHG, examining 141 locations worldwide7. In a more recent publication, the total worldwide GHG emissions and mitigation of PV deployment was evaluated from 2009 to 2019 and projected from 2020 to 20606. Furthermore, the global warming mitigation for rooftop was analyzed using worldwide data with a 1-km resolution16. These three studies used average grid emissions with a yearly resolution and acknowledged their limitations due to the daily and seasonal variability. The variation between using hourly and yearly resolution for GHG mitigation assessment was studied for a case in Spain, a hypothetical roof installation of 1 kWp was analyzed and the results for the hourly resolution GHG mitigation were 8% lower than the yearly one17. Besides these findings in Spain, a study on hourly resolution assessment of the GHG mitigation potential of PV deployment for multiple countries was not found during the literature review.

The analysis presented here is based on the premise that coordination for deployment could contribute to decarbonization goals6, and the strong collaboration around renewable energy within the EU11. The aim of this analysis is to quantify the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential of a 1 kWp PV system for each of the 27 EU countries, with an hourly resolution for the sake of more accurate results. The life-cycle GHG mitigation potential represents the cumulative lifetime GHG mitigation by summing the hourly mitigation (PV power generation times grid’s carbon intensity) across all operating hours. (for more details, see the Method section).

Life-cycle GHG mitigation potential

The results show a significant variation of life-cycle GHG mitigation potential within the analyzed locations, with the PV system in Cyprus having 31 times that of the system in Sweden due to the high solar irradiation and carbon-intensive electricity grid. The analysis of the relation of grid’s carbon intensity and PV generation with life-cycle GHG mitigation potential shows grid’s carbon intensity as the dominant factor for the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential. Moreover, the results are higher than the life-cycle GHG emissions of three PV systems obtained in a previous study18 for all cases except in Sweden and France, where one system (with simulated manufacturing in China) has higher life-cycle GHG emissions compared with the mitigation in these two countries. In addition to that, three different variations of the life-cycle GHG mitigation results are tested: (1) the difference between quantifying with hourly and yearly resolution, (2) projecting the results along the PV’s life-cycle with future grid decarbonization, and (3) the possible influence of negative electrical energy prices on the mitigation potential.

The main contribution of this study lies in the hourly resolution of the analyses, which increases the accuracy of the results compared with previous studies with similar objectives. From the analyses performed, the highest variation found for exponential decarbonization, the values can be up to 70% lower compared to a quantification that does not consider this factor. Despite the possible variations, the results of life-cycle GHG mitigation potential from PV could be used to coordinate its deployment within the EU to foster a faster decarbonization, leveraged by the already existing strong collaboration among these countries.

The life-cycle GHG mitigation potential is quantified for the 27 countries of the European Union, using average hourly grid carbon intensity and the energy generation from a simulated 1 kWp PV system. The results, in Fig. 1, show a significant variation between countries. The highest result is in Cyprus, where the mitigation potential is 18.6 t CO2e kWp−1, and the lowest one is in Sweden, with 0.6 t CO2e kWp−1. The remaining results for the 25 countries are between these two extremes, with an average of 6.3 t CO2e kWp−1.

The locations in the North (latitudes higher than a 53° latitude) show a relatively low GHG mitigation potential due to the low solar irradiation and relatively low-carbon grids. The exception is Ireland with 9.6 t CO2e kWp−1, caused by a relatively high carbon grid with a high reliance on gas turbines19. In the lower end are the Nordic countries with values ranging from 0.6 to 2.4 t CO2e kWp−1. The simple average for the Northern Europe group of countries (Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Lithuania and Sweden) is 3.8 t CO2e kWp−1, lower than the 5.8 t CO2e kWp−1 for mid-latitude locations.

The results for mid-latitude locations (latitudes between 48° and 53°) range from 0.8 t CO2e kWp−1 in France due to a high share of nuclear energy20 and 14.5 t CO2e kWp−1 in Poland, the second highest in the EU countries due to a carbon-intensive grid. The result for Germany is 6.4 t CO2e kWp−1, close to the average for the 27 EU countries (6.3 t CO2e kWp−1). The simple average for this group of countries is 5.8 t CO2e kWp−1, around 40% lower compared to the average of the Southern European countries, 8.2 t CO2e kWp−1.

Southern European locations (latitudes lower than 48°) have generally a higher PV generation, which influences the results of the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential. Portugal and Spain are on the west, and both have the lowest life-cycle GHG mitigation potential in this region with 3.4 t CO2e kWp−1 and 3.5 t CO2e kWp−1, respectively; despite high irradiation, and due to a relatively low-carbon grid compared to the rest of the countries in this group. The islands have the highest results, Malta with 13.8 t CO2e kWp−1 and Cyprus (the only country in the EU that is isolated from other grids21) with a life-cycle GHG mitigation potential of 18.6 t CO2e kWp−1, due to the combination of high PV power generation and a carbon-intensive grid. The rest of the southern European group is between 5 and 9 t CO2e kWp−1

Relating mitigation potential to PV and grid factors

To illustrate the influence of the grid’s carbon intensity and the PV generation on the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential, these variables are plotted in Fig. 2 with the PV penetration in 2024 from Ember’s European Electricity Review 202522. The analysis of these variables indicates that the grid’s carbon intensity is the predominant factor for the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential. The life-cycle GHG mitigation potential variates more along the carbon intensity (Y axis) compared with the annual PV generation (X axis) because the relative variation in the carbon intensity, encompassing more than 30-fold range (~700/22) is higher than the relative variation for the PV generation which is less than a 2-fold range (~1670/930). Figure 2 also shows PV penetration, this variable ranges from 1% in Finland to 24% in Hungary22. Cyprus, having the highest life cycle GHG mitigation potential has one of the highest PV penetration rates with almost 20%22.

GHG mitigation potential vs. PV system emissions

When the results previously shown are compared with the life-cycle GHG emissions from a PV system (including raw material extraction, manufacturing, transport, installation, and end of life), a conclusion about the net impact can be drawn. If the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential is higher than the life-cycle GHG emissions of a given PV system, a potential benefit towards decarbonization can be assumed. The life-cycle GHG mitigation potential compared with the emissions from three PV systems manufactured in China, Germany, and Norway (obtained from a recent study18) is presented in Fig. 3.

Comparing the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential with the life-cycle GHG emissions of three PV systems (modules with manufacturing simulated using the electricity mix of China, Germany, and Norway18) shows that the three PV systems have a theoretical decarbonization benefit in most locations. There are only two exceptions: the PV system from China has a global warming potential of 1.1 t CO2e kWp−1, 75% and 42% higher than the GHG mitigation potential of Sweden and France, respectively. For the remaining 25 countries, any of the three PV systems could theoretically contribute to the grid decarbonization, with up to 40 times more life-cycle GHG mitigation compared to the corresponding emissions of the PV system (Norwegian modules installed in Cyprus).

Hourly vs. yearly resolution in GHG mitigation potential

The results of quantifying the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential with yearly and hourly resolution are shown in Fig. 4. The results are similar for most countries, with two exceptions. The estimation with a yearly resolution is generally higher compared to a more accurate hourly resolution quantification, up to 49% higher for Cyprus. The two locations where the yearly quantification method gives higher results than the hourly obtained ones are Sweden and Ireland, with variations of −15% and −6% respectively. These differences can be explained by the daily and seasonal variation of both the solar energy generation from the 1 kWp system and the grid energy mix in the different countries.

The variation while using a yearly resolution (instead of hourly) to quantify the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential is generally higher for countries with a high solar energy penetration in their grids. This caused the grid carbon intensity to be lower when the PV system generation was high, making the periods of high PV generation account for less mitigation than if simply average yearly carbon intensities were used. This effect causes a higher variation in countries like the Netherlands (49%), Greece (48%), and Cyprus (41%). The average resolution variation for the 25 countries where the yearly estimation is higher than the hourly is 24%, considerably higher than the average for the opposite case, found in Sweden and Ireland (10%).

The two locations where the quantification with yearly average showed a lower life-cycle GHG mitigation potential are where the periods of high PV production have a higher or similar carbon intensity than other times during the year. This causes that periods with high PV generation account for more mitigation than if average yearly carbon intensities were used. This is the case for Sweden, where PV power generation has a higher lifecycle emissions factor than the average of the remaining energy sources in the grid, and in Ireland, where the patterns of wind power generation cause a slightly higher average carbon intensity during periods with high PV energy generation.

GHG mitigation potential under grid decarbonization

The life-cycle GHG mitigation potential changes depending on the scenario for future grid decarbonization used in the assessment of the 1 kWp PV system 25 years into the future, starting from 2024. The results shown previously do not assume any grid decarbonization; the hourly carbon intensity values from 2024 are assumed as the same 25 years into the future. Figure 5 shows the variation of the previous results with linear and exponential decarbonization paths based on the national net zero targets (as explained in the methods section). The decarbonization scenarios show lower GHG mitigation potential for the PV system, compaired with the no-decarbonizaiton assumption.

The exponential decarbonization assumption (a faster reduction of grid carbon intensity at the beginning) caused a higher reduction in the lifecycle GHG emissions mitigation compared to a linear (steady) decarbonization path. In general, a higher GHG mitigation potential causes a higher variation between the three decarbonization projections. For example, in Cyprus the variation is −40% and −70%, for the linear and exponential decarbonization, respectively. On the other hand, in France the results showed a variation of −23% for linear and −25% for exponential decarbonization. The variation in the results for both countries is significantly different, despite both having the same 2050 target year.

For countries with similar life-cycle GHG mitigation potential, the highest variation occurs when the net-zero targets are closer. For example, Finland and France have a lifecycle GHG mitigation without a decarbonization projection of 1.46 t CO2e kWp−1 and 0.78 t CO2e kWp−1 and net-zero targets in 2035 and 2050, respectively. The earlier target for Finland caused a lower lifecycle GHG mitigation than France when exponential decarbonization is projected, 0.55 t CO2e kWp−1 for Finland and 0.58 t CO2e kWp−1 for France. Other results more sensitive to decarbonization projection due to earlier targets are Germany and Sweden, with a net-zero target in 2045.

GHG mitigation potential considering electricity prices

If negative electrical energy prices are considered as a proxy for curtailment (non-decarbonization benefit) the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential is reduced, as shown in Fig. 6. This analysis is performed for all EU countries except Cyprus and Malta, due to the lack of publicly available hourly electricity prices. For the 25 remaining countries, the average reduction in lifecycle GHG mitigation is 8%, the highest reduction is 18% for Spain, and the lowest is 0% for Italy. The reduction in Spain is because there were 247 h of negative prices during 2024, while in Italy, there were no negative prices due to the regulation2.

This study explores the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential of a 1 kWp PV system, optimally oriented, installed in locations in each of the 27 EU countries. As in other studies, significant differences between countries were found, with high emissions and high irradiation countries having the highest mitigation7. If the results from this study are analyzed next to the PV added capacity during 20233, there is no obvious evidence of installation being prioritized in areas with high mitigation potential. This suggests that the current mechanisms to prioritize PV where it brings the biggest benefit, if any, might not be effective. Furthermore, PV deployment is driven by explicit renewable energy sources support policy, profitability of investment and certainty about the government’s long-term deployment intentions23, which are given by EU level policies and more importantly a set of national rules12. Therefore, these results could be used to inform a policy within the EU that prioritizes the countries where PV brings higher decarbonization benefits, as other studies have advocated for in a Worldwide level7.

The variation analyses confirm findings from previous studies with some differences. The variation between life-cycle GHG mitigation potential quantified with yearly average and hourly average emissions for Spain found in this study is 36% while for a previous reference it is 8%17. This variation could be explained by the energy mixes used; the previous study had 2021 mix data17, when the grid had a lower installed solar capacity. This study uses 2024 mix data from a grid with around double solar capacity, from 16 GWp (2021) to 31 GWp (2023)24. Also, the difference between estimating the mitigation potential with a constant future emissions factor and with decarbonization projections was found to be considerable. Assuming future decarbonization causes a variation of the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential that ranges from 14% to 70% lower than that assuming constant grid GHG. A previous study found a variation of around 27% between not assuming decarbonization and actual decarbonization during the period between 2009 to 20196. Regarding the negative electrical energy prices analysis, the results are higher than the publicly available curtailment rates with an average 8% reduction in the GHG mitigation potential, while official figures from IEA for curtailment are between 1.5% and 4%25. The availability of detailed, hourly curtailment data is a limitation for this analysis.

The conclusions from each of the analysis presented previously can serve as part of a broader decision support framework for practitioners and policy makers that considers the limitations of this study. For example, the regional differences in the lifecycle mitigation potential of PV systems can guide decision making on to where to deploy PV. However, this could imply additional challenges due to higher PV penetration like cannibalization effect (increasing renewable technologies’ penetration undermines their own value26) and requirements for flexibility to avoid grid instability27. For example, Cyprus (a special case) has the highest mitigation potential, yet also already has a relatively high PV penetration22, as does Greece22. Another finding from this study is the increase in accuracy that hourly (instead of yearly) resolution provides in the lifecycle GHG mitigation potential. Again, Cyprus’ results can serve as an example of the difference caused by the resolution of the calculation, because its relatively high PV penetration causes an overestimation (when using a yearly grid carbon intensity) of the GHG mitigation potential during high PV generation, typically lower carbon intensity intervals. Another contribution is the difference that estimating the mitigation potential with and without decarbonization makes, which depends on a projection that is inherently uncertain. Acknowledging and quantifying this uncertainty is also a practice that can help in understanding how today’s decisions might develop along the lifespan of a PV system being deployed in the present.

In this study, 27 PV systems are simulated using PVGIS with a specific configuration and considering only crystalline silicon module technology and PVGIS-SARAH2 surface radiation data record28. Therefore, only one point for every country is simulated, which might not comprehensively cover the performance diversity within each country due to technology, climate, and grid conditions. For example, temperature effects that are not fully captured can cause a variation of up to 10%, and this uncertainty increases if climate change is considered13. Furthermore, other simplifications made in the model, such as dust29, humidity, snow, albedo and atmospheric factors can affect the PV performance13. Moreover, all these factors, particularly the temperature can also affect the degradation of the PV modules, which in turn also affects the PV power generation over time14. Therefore, a future study with a higher geographic resolution16,30, more PV technologies7 and more accurate PV generation modeling can give more detailed insights into the GHG mitigation potential of PV in EU countries.

Another set of limitations arises from the assumptions around the life-cycle GHG emissions and mitigation. The analysis was performed with average hourly and yearly emissions, as if the energy generated from the PV would mitigate the GHG from an average unit of energy from the grid during that time. However, the mitigation can be related to the change in the energy system, usually called marginal energy, usually assumed to be more carbon-intensive due to the reduction of controllable, often fossil fuel energy sources, such as a gas turbine17. Furthermore, the PV energy could be displacing energy outside the electrical grid, including electric vehicles or electrified industry. Additionally, the growing adoption of battery storage alongside PV systems can shift the time of grid displacement, potentially altering the carbon intensity of the displaced electricity and thus the mitigation potential; this effect is not captured in the present analysis but warrants consideration in future studies. An application-based GHG mitigation for PV could be explored in future research in a similar way that was done for hydrogen31. However, the highly complex and dynamic nature of energy systems would cause estimating the marginal GHG emissions to carry more uncertainties than using a more conservative average quantification. Similarly, the embodied GHG taken from the literature18 are also subjected to change. For example, the grid emissions used for the manufacturing from China are potentially lowering the future due to the high rate of PV deployment4.

Despite the limitations and uncertainties in this study, the differences in life-cycle GHG mitigation of PV between countries are up to 10 to 30 times, if the results from Sweden and Cyprus are compared. The differences between countries have been found by more studies on a wider context and different methods6. Therefore, the results from this analysis could inform mechanisms for a coordinated deployment of PV, leveraged by the existing collaboration within the EU to achieve a faster decarbonization. These collaboration mechanisms could spread worldwide and help to achieve a more rapid climate change mitigation from PV systems globally.

Life-cycle assessment framework and study design

The framework for this study is lifecycle assessment (LCA) according to ISO 1404432. The main goal of the LCA is to determine the change environmental impact due to the installation of 1 kWp of PV in the EU countries. The system function is to provide the same electrical energy from the grid as the generated from a PV system across a lifespan of 25 years, hence the functional unit is a 1 kWp PV system with optimized orientation to maximize energy generation, operating for 25 years. The lifecycle scope is cradle to grave (raw material extraction, manufacturing, transport and end of life) and the geographical scope is one specific location per country in the EU. The coordinates of the locations and the optimal orientation and tilt (according to PVGIS) are shown in Table 1.

The lifecycle inventory includes the electrical AC energy from the grid, equivalent to the generated by a 1 kWp of PV across 25 years with 0.5% yearly degradation. The environmental impact assessment is done using electricity maps life-cycle emissions data for every hour33, which is obtained from the weighted average per energy source in the corresponding price zone using IPCC and UNECE life-cycle emission factor plus energy transmission from other price zones34. The environmental impact category used is the global warming potential (GWP), it quantifies the potential warming effects of GHG relative to carbon dioxide, one hundred years in the future35. The results of this LCA are referred to as “life-cycle GHG mitigation potential” within this text. The analysis of the results is done by comparing the 27 cases with each other plus four additional analyses: (1) comparative analysis of the results with the GWP of three PV systems with different manufacturing scenarios taken from the literature18, (2) variation analysis of the results with yearly resolution, (3) variation of the results with decarbonization scenarios, and (4) variation considering curtailment when prices are negative.

Figure 7 provides an overview of the methodology, which begins with data from 27 locations and concludes with the analyses presented in the previous figures. In the diagram, white shapes represent the analytical stages (which use referenced, simulated, and transformed data) while the colored shapes represent the main results plotted in each figure.

Average and life-cycle hourly power generation

To make the entire analysis, one location from each of the EU countries is selected36; the coordinates for the sites are shown in Table 1. These locations are used to simulate the hourly PV power generation from 2015 to 2020, for a 1 kWp system with optimal orientation using PVGIS28. From the six-year power generation data, the hourly power generation for an average year is obtained as shown:

$${P}_{h}^{{mean}}=\frac{1}{{y}_{p,n}-{y}_{p,0}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{y=y}_{p,0}}^{{y}_{p,n}}{P}_{h,y}$$

(1)

where Ph,y represents the power generated during each hour from 2015 to 2020 (expressed as yp,0 and yp,n respectively), y represents a given year within this range and \({P}_{h}^{{mean}}\) is the average hourly power generation across that period. From the average year, the lifecycle PV energy generation on an hourly basis is calculated for 25 years using a degradation of 0.5%, according to the following equation:

$${E}_{h}^{{lc}}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{y={y}_{0}}^{{y}_{n}}{(1+d)}^{y-{y}_{0}}\cdot {P}_{h}^{{mean}}$$

(2)

where d is the degradation and \({E}_{h}^{{lc}}\) is the lifecycle from y0 to yn (2024–2048) energy generated from the PV system during each hour on an average year. Having lifecycle hourly energy generation data facilitates further analysis.

Life-cycle GHG mitigation potential

To get the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential, the life-cycle energy generation data is multiplied by the hourly LCA GHG emissions for 2024, obtained for the corresponding grid area from electricity maps33, and summed as follows:

$${A}_{{lc}}^{{hr}}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{h=1}^{{h}_{n}}{E}_{h}^{{lc}}\cdot {G}_{h}$$

(3)

here \({G}_{h}\) is the LCA GHG for a given hour (h) during 2024 from h = 1 to hn (the last hour of the year), and \({A}_{{lc}}^{{hr}}\) represents the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential calculated with hourly resolution. These are the main results, and they are plotted in Fig. 1. The following analysis is a comparison between the lifecycle GHG mitigation potential and lifecycle GHG emissions from a previous study for a PV system with three manufacturing scenarios: Norway, Germany, and China18. The remaining three analyses are to explore possible variations of the assumptions made.

Variation analyses on life-cycle GHG mitigation potential

To illustrate possible variation in the results, due to different assumptions, three variation analyses were done: (1) Hourly and yearly resolution, (2) Negative price effects, and (3) Decarbonization scenarios. To analyze the difference between calculating with yearly resolution and hourly resolution, the theoretical mitigation with yearly resolution was obtained by multiplying the total energy generation (obtained from the sum of the life-cycle hourly generation) by the yearly 2024 LCA carbon intensity, as shown in the following equation:

$${A}_{{lc}}^{{yr}}={G}_{y}\cdot \mathop{\sum }\limits_{h=1}^{{h}_{n}}{E}_{h}^{{lc}}$$

(4)

where \({G}_{y}\) is the yearly greenhouse emissions of the given price area, and \({A}_{{lc}}^{{yr}}\) represents the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential calculated with yearly resolution. The negative price analysis is used as a proxy to estimate how much mitigation potential is lost due to curtailment. For this purpose, the GHG mitigation potential in a given hour is considered zero when the electricity price, for 2024 obtained from ENTSO-E37, is negative and not affected when the price is zero or positive. After these changes, the hourly mitigation potential is summed, as follows:

$${A}_{lc}^{hr,v}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{h=1}^{{h}_{n}}\left\{\begin{array}{ll}{E}_{h}^{lc}{\cdot G}_{h} & if\,{V}_{\,h} > 0\\ 0 & if\,{V}_{\,h}\le 0\,\end{array}\right.$$

(5)

here \({V}_{{h}}\) represents the electricity spot price for a given hour in 2024, and \({A}_{{lc}}^{{hr},v}\) is the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential calculated with hourly resolution, assuming no mitigation when prices are negative. The last variation analysis is done to explore how two different decarbonization paths could affect the results.

GHG mitigation potential under grid decarbonization

To analyze decarbonization scenarios, three additional assumptions are defined: (1) the decarbonization objective year, (2) the decarbonization path, and (3) the lifecycle GHG emission reached in the zero scenario. The decarbonization objective year is obtained from publicly available country or EU level goals. The most common goal year is 2050; however, Finland (2035)38, Austria (2040)39, Sweden (2045)40, and Germany (2045)41 are exceptions. For the decarbonization path, two functions are used: linear and exponential decarbonization. Finaly, for the minimum value achievable in the grid is taken from the report “Energy Pathways to 2050”, published by the French transmission system operator42. The value taken from this report is 16.3 g CO2e kWh−1, obtained from M1 scenario with focus on 100% renewable energy42, (10.5 Mt CO2e/645 TWh). The defined assumptions are combined to obtain the lifecycle GHG emissions mitigation under linear and exponential decarbonization scenarios as shown in Eqs. (7) and (9), respectively. Equation (6) is used to obtain the linear decarbonization fraction for a given year, as a previous step to get life-cycle GHG emissions mitigation with linear decarbonization, and it is defined as follows:

$${F}_{y}^{{lin}}=1+\left[\left(\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{y}_{g}-{y}_{0}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{{G}_{{zero}}}{{G}_{y}}-1\right)\right]$$

(6)

where \({G}_{{zero}}\) is the zero emissions floor (16.3 gCO2e kWh−1), yg is the decarbonization goal year, \({G}_{y}\) is the LCA GHG from the grid for 2024, and \({F}_{y}^{{lin}}\) is the fraction of the grid’s LCA GHG from 2024, for a in year y, under a linear decarbonization scenario. The result from Eq. (6) serves as input for the following equation:

$${A}_{{lc}}^{{lin},{hr}}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{y={y}_{0}}^{{y}_{n}}\left[{(1+d)}^{y-{y}_{0}}{\cdot F}_{y}^{{lin}}\cdot \mathop{\sum }\limits_{h=1}^{{h}_{n}}\left({P}_{h}^{{mean}}{\cdot G}_{h}\right)\right]$$

(7)

Here the result is \({A}_{{lc}}^{{lin},{hr}}\), representing the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential under a linear decarbonization scenario. The life-cycle GHG mitigation potential with exponential decarbonization is calculated using the following two equations: is used to get the exponential decarbonization fraction, defined as follows:

$${F}_{y}^{\exp }={\left(\frac{{G}_{{zero}}}{{G}_{y}}\right)}^{\left(\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{y}_{g}-{y}_{0}}\right)}$$

(8)

where the input variables are the same as for Eq. (6), and the result is the fraction of the lifecycle GHG emissions from the grid compared to that from 2024, for a given year, under an exponential decarbonization scenario expressed as \({{F}}_{y}^{\exp }\). The result obtained from Eq. (8) is used as input for Eq. (9), which is defined as:

$${A}_{{lc}}^{\exp ,{hr}}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{y={y}_{0}}^{{y}_{n}}\left[{\cdot (1+d)}^{y-{y}_{0}}\cdot {F}_{y}^{\exp }\cdot \mathop{\sum }\limits_{h=1}^{{h}_{n}}\left({P}_{h}^{{mean}}{\cdot G}_{h}\right)\right]$$

(9)

where \({A}_{{lc}}^{\exp ,{hr}}\) is the life-cycle GHG mitigation potential under an exponential decarbonization scenario.
